title: 09. Deep Learning: Classic CNN Architectures
summary: Learn the foundational CNN architectures that shaped computer vision: LeNet-5, AlexNet, and VGG. These architectures established the core principles used in modern deep learning.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
**Status:** ✅ COMPLETE  
**Last Updated:** December 6, 2025

Learn the foundational CNN architectures that shaped computer vision: **LeNet-5**, **AlexNet**, and **VGG**. These architectures established the core principles used in modern deep learning.

### What You'll Learn:
- LeNet-5 (1998) - First successful CNN
- AlexNet (2012) - ImageNet breakthrough
- VGGNet (2014) - Depth and simplicity
- Evolution of CNN design
- Implementation in PyTorch

sections.title: 1. LeNet-5 (1998)
sections.body:
### The First Successful CNN:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("LENET-5: THE PIONEER")
print("="*70)

print("""
LeNet-5 by Yann LeCun (1998)
Designed for: Handwritten digit recognition (MNIST)

Architecture:
   Input: 32×32 grayscale
   Conv1: 6 filters, 5×5 → 28×28×6
   Pool1: 2×2 avg pool → 14×14×6
   Conv2: 16 filters, 5×5 → 10×10×16
   Pool2: 2×2 avg pool → 5×5×16
   FC1: 120 neurons
   FC2: 84 neurons
   Output: 10 classes

Key Innovations:
   • First successful CNN
   • Convolutional feature extraction
   • Hierarchical learning
   • Shared weights (parameter efficiency)

Parameters: ~60K (tiny by today's standards!)
""")

class LeNet5(nn.Module):
    """LeNet-5 implementation."""
    
    def __init__(self, num_classes=10):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            # Conv1: 1→6 channels
            nn.Conv2d(1, 6, kernel_size=5, padding=2),
            nn.Tanh(),  # Original used tanh
            nn.AvgPool2d(2, 2),
            
            # Conv2: 6→16 channels
            nn.Conv2d(6, 16, kernel_size=5),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.AvgPool2d(2, 2)
        )
        
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(16 * 5 * 5, 120),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(120, 84),
            nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(84, num_classes)
        )
    
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.features(x)
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
        x = self.classifier(x)
        return x

# Create model
model = LeNet5()
print("\nLeNet-5 Architecture:")
print(model)

# Test
x = torch.randn(1, 1, 32, 32)
output = model(x)
print(f"\nInput: {x.shape} → Output: {output.shape}")

# Count parameters
total_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Total parameters: {total_params:,}")

print("="*70)
```

sections.title: 2. AlexNet (2012)
sections.body:
### The ImageNet Revolution:

```python
print("\n" + "="*70)
print("ALEXNET: THE BREAKTHROUGH")
print("="*70)

print("""
AlexNet by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Geoffrey Hinton (2012)
ImageNet 2012 Winner: 15.3% error (vs 26% runner-up)

Architecture:
   Input: 227×227×3 RGB
   Conv1: 96 filters, 11×11, stride=4 → 55×55×96
   MaxPool: 3×3, stride=2 → 27×27×96
   Conv2: 256 filters, 5×5 → 27×27×256
   MaxPool: 3×3, stride=2 → 13×13×256
   Conv3: 384 filters, 3×3 → 13×13×384
   Conv4: 384 filters, 3×3 → 13×13×384
   Conv5: 256 filters, 3×3 → 13×13×256
   MaxPool: 3×3, stride=2 → 6×6×256
   FC1: 4096 neurons
   FC2: 4096 neurons
   Output: 1000 classes

Key Innovations:
   ✅ ReLU activation (vs tanh/sigmoid)
   ✅ Dropout for regularization
   ✅ Data augmentation
   ✅ GPU training (2 GPUs in parallel)
   ✅ Local Response Normalization (LRN)
   ✅ Overlapping pooling

Impact:
   • Proved deep learning works at scale
   • Started deep learning revolution
   • Showed importance of depth and data

Parameters: ~60 million
""")

class AlexNet(nn.Module):
    """AlexNet implementation (simplified)."""
    
    def __init__(self, num_classes=1000):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            # Conv1: Large receptive field
            nn.Conv2d(3, 96, kernel_size=11, stride=4, padding=2),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2),
            
            # Conv2
            nn.Conv2d(96, 256, kernel_size=5, padding=2),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2),
            
            # Conv3
            nn.Conv2d(256, 384, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            
            # Conv4
            nn.Conv2d(384, 384, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            
            # Conv5
            nn.Conv2d(384, 256, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2),
        )
        
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Dropout(0.5),
            nn.Linear(256 * 6 * 6, 4096),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Dropout(0.5),
            nn.Linear(4096, 4096),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Linear(4096, num_classes),
        )
    
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.features(x)
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
        x = self.classifier(x)
        return x

# Create model
model = AlexNet()
print("\nAlexNet Architecture:")
for name, module in model.named_children():
    print(f"\n{name}:")
    print(module)

# Test
x = torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224)
output = model(x)
print(f"\nInput: {x.shape} → Output: {output.shape}")

# Count parameters
total_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Total parameters: {total_params:,}")

print("="*70)
```

sections.title: 3. VGGNet (2014)
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- VGGNet by Karen Simonyan & Andrew Zisserman (2014) ImageNet 2014: 2nd place (7.3% error)
- VGG-16 implementation.
- Block 1: 64 channels
- Block 2: 128 channels
- Block 3: 256 channels
- Block 4: 512 channels
- Block 5: 512 channels

### Depth Through Simplicity:

```python
print("\n" + "="*70)
print("VGGNET: GOING DEEPER")
print("="*70)

print("""
VGGNet by Karen Simonyan & Andrew Zisserman (2014)
ImageNet 2014: 2nd place (7.3% error)

Philosophy:
   "Deeper is better, keep it simple"
   • Only 3×3 convolutions
   • Only 2×2 max pooling
   • Double channels after each pool
   • Very deep (16-19 layers)

VGG-16 Architecture:
   Input: 224×224×3
   
   Block 1: Conv3-64, Conv3-64, MaxPool → 112×112×64
   Block 2: Conv3-128, Conv3-128, MaxPool → 56×56×128
   Block 3: Conv3-256, Conv3-256, Conv3-256, MaxPool → 28×28×256
   Block 4: Conv3-512, Conv3-512, Conv3-512, MaxPool → 14×14×512
   Block 5: Conv3-512, Conv3-512, Conv3-512, MaxPool → 7×7×512
   
   FC1: 4096
   FC2: 4096
   Output: 1000

Key Insights:
   ✅ Two 3×3 convs = receptive field of one 5×5
      (but fewer parameters!)
   ✅ Uniform architecture (easy to understand)
   ✅ Proved depth is crucial
   ✅ Standard building block: Conv→Conv→Pool

Why 3×3 Convolutions?
   • Two 3×3 = receptive field 5×5
     Params: 2 × (3×3×C×C) = 18C²
   • One 5×5:
     Params: 5×5×C×C = 25C²
   • Savings: 28% fewer parameters!
   • More non-linearity (2 ReLUs vs 1)

Parameters: ~138 million (VGG-16)
""")

class VGG16(nn.Module):
    """VGG-16 implementation."""
    
    def __init__(self, num_classes=1000):
        super().__init__()
        
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            # Block 1: 64 channels
            nn.Conv2d(3, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),
            
            # Block 2: 128 channels
            nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(128, 128, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),
            
            # Block 3: 256 channels
            nn.Conv2d(128, 256, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(256, 256, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(256, 256, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),
            
            # Block 4: 512 channels
            nn.Conv2d(256, 512, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(512, 512, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(512, 512, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),
            
            # Block 5: 512 channels
            nn.Conv2d(512, 512, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(512, 512, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(512, 512, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2),
        )
        
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(512 * 7 * 7, 4096),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Dropout(0.5),
            nn.Linear(4096, 4096),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Dropout(0.5),
            nn.Linear(4096, num_classes),
        )
    
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.features(x)
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
        x = self.classifier(x)
        return x

# Create model
model = VGG16()
print("\nVGG-16 Architecture Summary:")
print(f"Feature extractor: {len([m for m in model.features if isinstance(m, nn.Conv2d)])} conv layers")
print(f"Classifier: {len([m for m in model.classifier if isinstance(m, nn.Linear)])} FC layers")

# Test
x = torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224)
output = model(x)
print(f"\nInput: {x.shape} → Output: {output.shape}")

# Count parameters
total_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Total parameters: {total_params:,}")

print("="*70)
```

sections.title: 4. Architecture Comparison
sections.body:
### Evolution of CNNs:

```python
print("\n" + "="*70)
print("CLASSIC CNN COMPARISON")
print("="*70)

comparison = """
┌──────────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
│ Property     │ LeNet-5  │ AlexNet  │ VGG-16   │
├──────────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
│ Year         │ 1998     │ 2012     │ 2014     │
│ Depth        │ 7 layers │ 8 layers │ 16 layers│
│ Parameters   │ 60K      │ 60M      │ 138M     │
│ Input Size   │ 32×32    │ 227×227  │ 224×224  │
│ Dataset      │ MNIST    │ ImageNet │ ImageNet │
│ Accuracy     │ 99.05%   │ 84.7%    │ 92.7%    │
│ GPU Days     │ N/A      │ 5-6 days │ 2-3 weeks│
└──────────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘

Key Innovations:

LeNet-5 (1998):
   • First working CNN
   • Proved concept of hierarchical features
   • Used tanh activation
   • Average pooling
   
AlexNet (2012):
   • ReLU activation
   • Dropout regularization
   • Data augmentation
   • GPU training
   • Max pooling
   • Large kernels (11×11)
   
VGG-16 (2014):
   • All 3×3 convolutions
   • Very deep (16 layers)
   • Simple, uniform architecture
   • Proved depth matters
   • Modular design (VGG blocks)

Lessons Learned:
1. Depth improves performance
2. Small kernels (3×3) are efficient
3. ReLU > tanh/sigmoid
4. Dropout prevents overfitting
5. Data augmentation is crucial
6. More parameters ≠ better (diminishing returns)
"""

print(comparison)

print("\n📈 Performance vs Parameters:")
print("-" * 70)
models = [
    ("LeNet-5", 0.06, 99.05, "MNIST"),
    ("AlexNet", 60, 84.7, "ImageNet top-5"),
    ("VGG-16", 138, 92.7, "ImageNet top-5"),
]

for name, params_m, acc, dataset in models:
    print(f"{name:<15} {params_m:>6.1f}M params  {acc:>5.2f}%  ({dataset})")

print("="*70)
```

sections.title: 5. Training These Models
sections.body:
### Practical Tips:

```python
print("\n" + "="*70)
print("TRAINING CLASSIC CNNS")
print("="*70)

training_code = """
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from torchvision import datasets, transforms

# ============================================================
# TRAINING LENET-5 ON MNIST
# ============================================================

# Data
transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.Resize(32),  # LeNet expects 32×32
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize((0.1307,), (0.3081,))
])

train_data = datasets.MNIST('./data', train=True, download=True, transform=transform)
train_loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train_data, batch_size=64, shuffle=True)

# Model
model = LeNet5().cuda()
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001)

# Training loop (1 epoch)
model.train()
for batch_idx, (data, target) in enumerate(train_loader):
    data, target = data.cuda(), target.cuda()
    
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    output = model(data)
    loss = criterion(output, target)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    
    if batch_idx % 100 == 0:
        print(f'Batch {batch_idx}, Loss: {loss.item():.4f}')

# ============================================================
# TRAINING ALEXNET/VGG ON IMAGENET
# ============================================================

# Data augmentation (critical for ImageNet)
train_transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.RandomResizedCrop(224),
    transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(),
    transforms.ColorJitter(brightness=0.2, contrast=0.2),
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize([0.485, 0.456, 0.406], [0.229, 0.224, 0.225])
])

# Model
model = VGG16(num_classes=1000).cuda()
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

# Optimizer settings (from original papers)
optimizer = optim.SGD(
    model.parameters(),
    lr=0.01,  # Initial LR
    momentum=0.9,
    weight_decay=5e-4
)

# Learning rate schedule
scheduler = optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(optimizer, step_size=30, gamma=0.1)

# Training tips:
# 1. Start with lower LR (0.01) and reduce by 10× every 30 epochs
# 2. Use SGD with momentum (Adam can work but SGD generalizes better)
# 3. Heavy data augmentation
# 4. Batch size: as large as GPU allows (128-256)
# 5. Train for 90+ epochs
# 6. Use dropout in FC layers
"""

print(training_code)

print("\n💡 Training Recommendations:")
print("""
LeNet-5 (MNIST):
   • Optimizer: Adam, lr=0.001
   • Epochs: 10-20
   • Batch size: 64
   • No augmentation needed
   • Trains in minutes

AlexNet (ImageNet):
   • Optimizer: SGD, lr=0.01, momentum=0.9
   • Epochs: 90
   • Batch size: 256
   • Heavy augmentation
   • Weight decay: 5e-4
   • Trains in days

VGG-16 (ImageNet):
   • Same as AlexNet
   • May need gradient clipping
   • Consider smaller batch size (GPU memory)
   • Trains in weeks

Modern Improvements:
   • Use BatchNorm (faster convergence)
   • Use AdamW instead of SGD
   • Cosine annealing LR schedule
   • Mixed precision training (2× speedup)
   • Warmup for first few epochs
""")

print("="*70)
```

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
### Classic CNN Architectures:

| Architecture | Year | Key Innovation | Parameters |
|-------------|------|----------------|------------|
| **LeNet-5** | 1998 | First successful CNN | 60K |
| **AlexNet** | 2012 | ReLU, Dropout, GPU | 60M |
| **VGG-16** | 2014 | 3×3 convs, depth | 138M |

### Design Principles:

```
LeNet-5:  Conv → Pool → Conv → Pool → FC → FC
AlexNet:  Large kernels → Max pool → Smaller kernels → FC
VGG:      Many 3×3 convs → Max pool → Deeper is better
```

### Legacy:

These architectures laid the foundation for modern CNNs. While no longer state-of-the-art, understanding them is essential for appreciating advances like ResNet and EfficientNet.

**Next Topic:** ResNet - The architecture that changed everything! 🚀
